after.name: Question 1
after.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(0.5,1)$ to $(0,2).$
after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0.5,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(0.5,1) & =2\cdot 0.5\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0.5+Δx,1+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+1\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(0.5,1)$ to $(0,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0-0.5=-0.5, \\ Δy & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+1\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-0.5)+1\cdot (1) \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $0.5.$

after.problem: Estimate $\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.2)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ at the point $(4,1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(4,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡1}{2\sqrt{4}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{\sqrt{4}}{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(4+Δx,1+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.2)=f(3.9,1.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3.9,1.2).$

Moving from $(4,1)$ to $(3.9,1.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3.9-4=-0.1, \\ Δy & =1.2-1=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (-0.1)+2\cdot (0.2) \\  & ≈0+0.4 \\  & ≈0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.4.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.9,1.2) & ≈f(4,1)+0.4 \\ \sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.2) & ≈\sqrt{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡1+0.4 \\  & ≈0+0.4 \\  & ≈0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(4,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡1}{2\sqrt{4}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{\sqrt{4}}{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(4+Δx,1+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.2)=f(3.9,1.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3.9,1.2).$

Moving from $(4,1)$ to $(3.9,1.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3.9-4=-0.1, \\ Δy & =1.2-1=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (-0.1)+2\cdot (0.2) \\  & ≈0+0.4 \\  & ≈0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.4.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.9,1.2) & ≈f(4,1)+0.4 \\ \sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.2) & ≈\sqrt{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡1+0.4 \\  & ≈0+0.4 \\  & ≈0.4.\end{aligned}

Given a right cone, find the differential dS for the lateral surface area S of the right cone if the base radius is r=6, and the slant height is l=10.

a
 10πdr+6πdl
b
 10dr+6dl
c
 40πdr+12πdl
d
 12dr+40dl

 6πdr+10πdl
Submit

decision.explanation: The lateral surface area is S=πrl, so dS=πl dr+πr dl. Substituting r=6 and l=10 gives dS=10π dr+6π dl.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Given a right cone, find the differential $\text{d}S$ for the lateral surface area $S$ of the right cone if the base radius is $r=6,$ and the slant height is $l=10.$
after.worked_solution:
The  lateral surface area of the right cone is $S=\pi rl.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(rl) & =(\frac{∂S}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂S}{∂l})\,\text{d}l \\  & =\pi l\,\text{d}r+\pi r\,\text{d}l\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=6,$ and $l=10,$  the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}S(6,10) & =10\pi \,\text{d}r+6\pi \,\text{d}l.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: If $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{3}-y),$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2).$
after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12{z}^{2}}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,-3,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,-3,1) & =(2\cdot 2)\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12\cdot {1}^{2}}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}z \\  & =4\,\text{d}x-\,\text{d}y+3\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,-3+Δy,1+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx-\,Δy+3\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-2=-1, \\ Δy & =-2-(-3)=1 \\ Δz & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\,Δx-1\,Δy+3\,Δz \\  & ≈4\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1+3\cdot 1 \\  & ≈-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ decreases by approximately $-2.$
